title: The Fewest Jumps to Reach the Last Square

concept.title: Jump only when you must: remember how far the current jump reaches and how far the next one could
body: You stand on the first of `n` squares in a row. From the square `i` you can jump **any distance from 1 up to `a[i]`** to the right. What is the **smallest number of jumps** that brings you to the last square? For `2 3 1 1 4` the answer is 2: jump 1 square, then 3 squares. It is guaranteed that the end can be reached.

Think in *rounds*. After `k` jumps you can stand on any square from the start up to some farthest square, call it `cur_end`. While walking over the squares of the current round, keep `farthest`, the farthest square reachable from any of them with **one more jump**. When the walk reaches `cur_end` — the end of the current round — one more jump is needed, and after it the new reachable block ends at `farthest`: `jumps += 1`, `cur_end = farthest`. This is a breadth-first search in which a round is one level, but because the reachable squares always form a block, we only need two numbers.

body.code:
jumps = cur_end = farthest = 0
for i in range(n - 1):                 # the last square needs no jump from itself
    farthest = max(farthest, i + a[i])
    if i == cur_end:                   # the round is over: we must jump now
        jumps += 1
        cur_end = farthest
print(jumps)

body: Why is delaying the jump until the end of the round right? Any square of the round could be the one we jump from, and the one that reaches farthest is at least as good as the others, so the choice can be made afterwards, when we know `farthest`. This makes the algorithm one pass, O(n), instead of the O(n^2) table of "fewest jumps to each square". (The earlier question "can the end be reached at all?" was solved with just the farthest reach.)

statement: There are `n` squares in a row and you start on the first one. From the square `i` you may jump to any square from `i + 1` to `i + a[i]`. Print the smallest number of jumps needed to reach the last square (0 if there is only one square). It is guaranteed that the last square can be reached.
inputFormat: The first line has `n`: the number of squares.
The second line has `n` numbers: `a[i]` is the longest jump you may make from the square `i`.
outputFormat: Print the smallest number of jumps.
constraints: The last square can always be reached.

examples.note: Jump from the square 0 to 1, then 3 squares to the end: 2 jumps.
You are already on the last square: 0.

hints: Treat the squares reachable with k jumps as a block that ends at cur_end.
While scanning the block, keep the farthest square that one more jump can reach.
At the end of the block count a jump and move cur_end to that farthest square.

starter.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n = int(input())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))

# Your code here

explanation: The squares reachable with k jumps form a block ending at cur_end; while scanning the block the farthest square reachable with one more jump is kept, and at the end of the block a jump is counted and cur_end becomes that farthest square.

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n = int(input())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))

jumps = cur_end = farthest = 0
for i in range(n - 1):
    if i + a[i] > farthest:
        farthest = i + a[i]
    if i == cur_end:
        jumps += 1
        cur_end = farthest
print(jumps)
